speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-119, to amend the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is being introduced at the present time because I have recently had my attention drawn to the case of a naturalized Canadian citizen of German origin with a Canadian born wife and three Canadian born children who is obliged to live abroad by the nature of his employment as one of the greatest living authorities in his field. Unless the law is changed this Canadian citizen will be deprived of his citizenship under section 18 of the citizenship act, though no similar penalty would attach to a natural born Canadian citizen in the same circumstances.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask whether it is a fact that the under secretary of state has handed in his resignation and, if so, on what date?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day when a question was asked in this regard I said I had no knowledge of this matter. I became aware only on Saturday that the resignation was being considered. I received today a letter dated July 1, 1961, written by the under secretary of state, and with the leave of the house I shall read that letter:
Ottawa, July 1, 1961
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,
As I wish to return to private practice of law, I hereby tender to you, and through you, to his excellency the governor general in council, my resignation, to become effective on September 5, 1961, as under secretary of state and deputy registrar general and also as member of the copyright appeal board. I would refer in this connection to sections 3 (1) and 6 (1) of the Department of State Act, c. 77 R.S.C. 1952, to section 50 of the Copyright Act, c. 55 R.S.C. 1952, to order in council P.C. 265, of January 19, 1949 and to order in council P.C. 2283, of May 9, 1949.
As the Secretary of State well knows, the only reason for my resignation is my desire to take advantage of an offer, which I consider quite interesting, to return to law practice. I think I can say that my relations with you, with my minister

and his predecessors and with the government generally and my own colleagues have been excellent. No wonder, therefore, that it was with considerable hesitation and regret that I took the decision which I did. I shall always cherish the memory of my nearly twenty-three years' service with the government of Canada (more than ten in the Department of Justice and the rest in the Department of the Secretary of State), to which I owe invaluable training and knowledge.
I would like, incidentally, to take this opportunity to thank you and the government for the recent increase in my salary. It is perhaps an unfortunate coincidence that I reached my decision to resign soon thereafter.
I sincerely thank you, sir, and your colleagues for the confidence with which you have honoured me.
Yours very truly, Charles Stein.
P.S.: Though I have marked this letter "Confidential", I need hardly say that, as far as I am concerned, you are quite at liberty, sir, to quote it publicly in whole or In part, should you deem it appropriate.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Forestry. In view of the disastrous fires raging in the forests of northwestern Ontario, with half a million acres involved, including the destruction of various logging and tourist camps and the closing of five mines in the Red Lake district, is the minister in a position to inform the house whether his department has taken any measure of assistance to the area?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Flemming (Minister of Forestry):
speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the courtesy of the hon. gentleman in sending me a copy of the question. I can quite understand his interest, concern, and even anxiety in connection with the very serious situation referred to in his question. The official answer, I might say, is as follows.
The Department of Forestry has not participated directly in fighting forest fires in the area referred to. Our contribution to the provinces in forest fire protection has been restricted to research programs and financial assistance under the agreements toward capital expenditures required for fire protection, including purchase of equipment, construction of ranger stations, lookout towers, roads and trails and the like. We are watching the situation with great concern, but up to date no representations have been received from the province of Ontario, which is responsible for the protection of its forests, for any extra assistance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs based upon a United Press report that instructions were agreed upon by the British and Soviet co-chairmen on Saturday after seven weeks of hassling, and that a move to give the international control commission of Laos more air and ground equipment to supervise the cease fire ran into new trouble yesterday when Canadian objections stopped the fresh instructions half way to Vientiane.
Is the minister in a position to say that the basis for the Canadian objection was as further reported, that the instructions given by the two co-chairmen would have afforded to one member of the commission a veto that, in the opinion of Canada, would have limited the successful operation of the commission in Laos?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REPORTED CANADIAN OBJECTIONS TO INSTRUCTIONS TO COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday of last week the co-chairmen met with the representatives of Canada, India and Poland to discuss the provision of helicopters, 

light aircraft, road transport and other essential equipment for the truce supervisory commission in Laos. At this meeting the Canadian representative took the position that the commission should be given the authority to obtain the equipment it requires from whatever source it considers best, by purchase if necessary and that such equipment must be entirely under the commission's control and at its disposal at all times.
Newspaper accounts of the results of that meeting are misleading in that they indicate that agreement had been reached by the co-chairmen that equipment would be under the commission's own control. The implication was that the commission was to be provided with equipment, but in fact all that happened at the meeting was a co-chairmen's decision to send yet another request for information to Vientiane without taking any practical steps to make equipment available. In addition, the objectional features were retained, namely the dependence upon the agreement of the parties in Laos and the failure to take cognizance of offers already made. I refer to the offers by the United States and by France.
The Canadian representative has continued to argue vigorously that steps should be taken to enable the commission to obtain the essential equipment it needs without further delay so that it may be in a position to carry out an effective supervision of the cease-fire. As I pointed out earlier, both at Geneva and in my statement to the house on June 23, the commission would be rendered impotent and ineffective if it is made dependent on the Laotian parties for the transport it requires to carry out its task.
The government is continuing its efforts to ensure that suitable arrangements are made to provide the commission with the aircraft and other equipment it requires. The responsibility for providing this equipment rests, of course, on the two co-chairmen of the Geneva conference, namely the United Kingdom and the Soviet union. There must be clear-cut action on their part if equipment is to be supplied, and supplied under the control of the commission. Canada will do her best to see that this commission functions effectively, but under present conditions the Canadian people would be quite wrong to expect that the commission can do its job properly.

What we are trying to reach and penalize here is the practice of some persons of writing insurance on property or risks in Canada with companies that are not authorized1 to do business in Canada, or with companies that are authorized to do business in Canada but through persons who are not agents qualified to do business in Canada.
I dealt with this problem in the budget speech. We have reason to believe that something of this kind has been going on. We have not been able to ascertain precisely its scale, but it is enough to have given rise to strong representations from insurance agents as well as insurance companies lawfully authorized to do business in Canada.
I point out that if the result of this proposed tax to be applied in such cases were to yield a substantial revenue it would not accomplish the result we are seeking to achieve here, because we wish to put a stop to a practice that we think is very unfair and improper.

I thank the minister for his explanation. That is what I wanted him to state for the record. I think I can properly add the comment that the section is mainly applicable to fire insurance and automobile insurance, as I understand it. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is to apply to all classes of insurance with the exceptions stated here, which are life insurance, personal accident insurance, sickness insurance or insurance against marine risks, and insurance against nuclear risks to the extent that such insurance against nuclear risks is not available in Canada.
And to clear up the situation in order to protect Canadian insurance companies and Canadian underwriters; that is the purpose of the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. There is reason to believe that Canadian companies are losing premiums and Canadian insurance agents are losing commissions that they would otherwise gain if this business were properly written in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister indicated that he felt it is related to recent discussions held at a high level
[Mr. Mcllraith.)
across the country concerning foreign ownership of some of our important corporations. Did the minister indicate that he felt perhaps some of our foreign owned corporations had ignored Canadian insurance opportunities and had rather automatically, on a package basis, insured their Canadian subsidiaries through their own foreign insurance agencies, and this is a step to discourage that practice? Is that part of the aim of this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It certainly is. It is designed to do more than discourage that, Mr. Chairman; it is designed to put a stop, as far as it is possible to do so, to the writing of insurance outside Canada on risks of this kind in Canada, either through companies that are not authorized to do business in Canada or through companies that are authorized to do business in Canada but through agents who are not authorized to do business in Canada. I dealt with the matter, I think rather fully, in the budget speech. It is to be found at page 6663 of Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister indicate whether he has considered the application of this amendment in a particular way to, say, the Allstate company, which I think is a subsidiary of Sears-Roe-buck of the United States? We discussed the inroads of this company in the insurance business in the estimates committee. Would the minister say whether this type of business, which undertakes insurance offerings in a retail store, in its relationship to Canadian consumers, is involved in the amendments before us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think it would be proper on my part to comment on the business operations of any particular company designated by name. In the budget speech I think I made quite clear the circumstances which have given rise to this amendment and the purposes that we have in mind. I said:
There appears to be an Increasing tendency on the part of non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada, and also Canadian corporations which are controlled outside of Canada, to arrange their fire and casualty insurance in respect of risks in Canada either with insurers which are not authorized to transact the business of insurance in Canada or with insurers that are so authorized but through agents or brokers located outside Canada. Undoubtedly these practices stem from a desire to make all insurance arrangements at the head office of the corporation or at the head office of the parent corporation, as the case may be, rather than from any lack of adequate insurance facilities in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, surely the minister has given consideration to the number of people who have insured themselves

through the Allstate company, shall I say as one illustration? I understand that one of our prominent business houses, the ex Robert Simpson company, by reason of an association with the Sears organization in Toronto, provides a retail store service selling automobile insurance. It has made some progress in selling insurance which I understand is really taken care of finally by the head office in Chicago. Will this service be affected, and does this measure relate to insurance policies that have been purchased by a great number of Canadians from the Allstate company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that would depend on the extent to which the company in question is authorized and licensed to do business in Canada, and the extent to which those individuals who are transacting the business immediately over the counter are so authorized and qualified.
Clauses 1 to 3 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 4.
With respect to clause 4, I take it we can discuss anything which can be discussed under it under clause 7?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is right, and I think clause 7 is the better clause for the discussion which my hon. friend has in mind.
Clauses 4 and 5 agreed to.
On clause 6-Joint and several ability of licensed purchaser and vendor.

Mr. Chairman, with reference to clause 6 would the parliamentary secretary tell me when section 68 was added to the act? Perhaps I could indicate the basis for asking that question, which is that I have before me what purports to be an up to date act, but it does not include this section.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the only information I have in this regard has relation to the marginal note in the last consolidation which shows it as new in 1959; chapter 23, section 10.

If the parliamentary secretary has it before him and it is not too lengthy, I wonder if he would mind reading it. I obtained what I thought was the excise tax act with amendments up to date but section 68 is not included.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman like section 68 put on the record?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 68 reads as follows:
Where a purchaser of goods from a wholesaler, producer, manufacturer or importer has falsely represented that the goods were intended for a
Excise Tax Act
use rendering them exempt from tax under any provision of this act, the wholesaler, producer, manufacturer or importer, as the case may be is entitled to recover from the purchaser the taxes paid by him under this act in respect of those goods.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 7.

Mr. Chairman, in respect to clause 7 the committee will note, as has been noted by the observations of the member for Ottawa West, that we are a little short of information on the righthand page of the bill, because clause 7 says:
Section 1 of schedule I to the said act is repealed.
There is no explanatory note in this regard. In view of the fact that this bill has come to us, as all will admit, with very little advance notice, perhaps the parliamentary secretary will now provide that information which is not provided in the bill, and perhaps in particular, in respect to subclause 2 of clause 7, he could indicate the volume of trade relating to these lighters, because I understand there is an increase in the protection which will provide that the duty in no case will be less than 10 cents per article. Perhaps he could also indicate who will be affected in our trade relations by this proposal and the volume of business we do, not only on the export side but on the import side, with the important trading nations involved?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as a result of the hon. member's experience as parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance, I am sure he will remember that it has never been the practice to provide explanatory notes in relation to schedules of bills. It has been the uniform practice not to put in explanatory notes. In fact the budget resolutions which precede such bills are the explanatory notes. I will be glad to draw my hon. friend's attention to the particular budget resolution which applies in each case. Subclause 2 to which he refers, relates to resolution No. 4.
The hon. member has asked a question in relation to the volume of trade and I might say that in recent years the average has been just under or over 5 million lighters sold each year. I have the breakdown here for the three years 1957, 1958 and 1959. I will give these figures indicating the year, the imports, the domestic production and then the totals. In 1957 the imports amounted to 3,747,924 and the domestic to 618,869, totalling 4,364,793; 1958, 4,145,292 and 541,266, making a total of 4,686,558.

I take it the second figure relates to domestic?

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, the second figure relates to domestic. In 1959 imports amounted to 4,714,800 and the domestic to 642,182, making a total of 5,356,982.
Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary did not indicate our trading partner which might be most affected by this proposed change.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think our imports are mainly from Japan and the United States.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the parliamentary secretary could tell us what the range of cost is in regard to these items, because the impact of the import will vary and will depend a good deal upon the sale price average.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my understanding is that the average duty paid value of an imported lighter is in the vicinity of 25 cents, while the average value of a Canadian made lighter is about $1.60. In respect to domestic lighters under the general rate of 10 per cent the excise tax has been as much as six to seven times the amount which was borne by imported lighters.
In other words what the government is seeking to do here is to impose something more in the nature of a specific tax rather than a percentage tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is endeavouring to equalize the situation as between imported and domestic lighters.
It amounts to a 40 per cent tax.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 8.

Mr. Chairman, in respect to this clause I should like to say a word or two regarding two articles mentioned on page 5 of the bill, shingles and prepared roofing for buildings. In the district which I represent we grow a very high quality red cedar and there has developed in recent years quite a good industry for the sale of split cedar shakes- not singles, but split cedar shakes. Would those split cedar shakes which are sold commercially to people who want to build in most instances quite expensive homes, and are very popular, be considered as shingles or as prepared roofing for buildings?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I say to the hon. gentleman that the only change made in this particular part of the schedule is to delete therefrom the word "doors". As it previously read it was "lumber, sash, doors." Doors are being eliminated and, as the hon. gentleman will see by reference to page 4, are put in a separate category with door and window

screens. Therefore there is no change in the situation. As to the particular matter to which the hon. gentleman refers, I am told that in any event they would be exempt.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister with respect to the items mentioned here, which of course vary a great deal. In view of the fact that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River indicated at the resolution stage, in the cooperation we extended at that time that we would expect full explanation of these items on the bill, I think we should take each of the items separately and have an explanation of each from the parliamentary secretary so we can see what the real implications are and so that there will be something on Hansard for the public to see.

That was part of my purpose originally. We are dealing with building materials in clause 8. I think the officers of the Canadian Construction Association have indicated that these professed reductions in taxation are really inconsequential to that industry. They may be valuable in that they conform to reductions which have taken place in the past and therefore there is no disagreement between one type of product that goes into construction and another. But in so far as any expansionist program of the government is concerned in its tax reductions announced in the current budget, what actual expansion is likely to occur in trade and in production of those items which are referred to under the heading of building materials?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if it is the wish of the committee to adopt the suggestion of the hon. gentleman from Bona-vista-Twillingate I think it would be satisfactory. The changes, of course, in this schedule are only those which are indicated in the bill by the black marginal line. We might, if it is the wish of the committee, deal with each of those separately. My hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River has suggested that these are not of great value.
I say the construction industry president said that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: With that I would take immediate issue and say many of these are of very substantial value to the building industry, as will be apparent as we go along. My hon. friend chooses to use the word "expansionist". This is a word which I venture to suggest to him applies, and applies very vividly, to the whole of this budget. These are only part of the whole budget which in its essence is the word he used.

The parliamentary secretary has mentioned an expansionist budget. Of course he could not have chosen a more opportune time to use that word, since the first word in this clause is "blowers". Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would do a little blowing and show just precisely what the expansion is in "blowers for use in warm air systems for the heating of buildings". This is the expression used in the clause. I think it may be appropriate because I suspect, sir, that is a pretty good description of this expansionist budget.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall clause 8
carry?
I thought the parliamentary secretary was going to explain this item.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I shall be glad to. The particular change here relates to blowers for use in warm air systems for the heating of buildings. This subclause proposes to make all blowers used in warm air heating systems unconditionally exempt from sales tax. The present administrative practice is that such blowers when sold with furnaces are regarded as a component of these furnaces and held to be exempt from sales tax. This is because schedule III provides a sales tax exemption for furnaces for the heating of buildings. However, the recent change in the form of construction of some of the warm air heating systems puts the blower in the duct work some distance away from the furnace. As a result the blower is purchased separately and is no longer regarded as a part of the furnace, and thus it becomes taxable. The proposed exemption specifically mentioning blowers will ensure that all blowers receive the same sales tax treatment whether sold with or without furnaces.
This is likely to mean a revenue loss of $40,000 approximately. As the committee will see, really what it does is to remove an anomaly that arises by reason of the new type of hot air furnace.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 8 carry?
No. I thought we were going to call these items one by one?
Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of questions referring to page 6 of this clause.

Would my hon. friend not agree that we should take them up consecutively? We have taken blowers; now we come to doors. I think we would make much more progress if we could do this consecutively. If Your Honour would refer to each of the items, perhaps by the first word, then we could have an explanation from the parliamentary secretary about what it involves,
Excise Tax Act
because there was no debate at the resolution stage and there really ought to be an explanation in Hansard of what is involved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The next item deals with doors for buildings and door and window screens. This is purely for clarification purposes and to make clear that the doors are doors for buildings. It was put in previously with lumber, sash and so on, and doubt arose as to whether other forms of doors were included or whether it was simply doors for buildings.
What other forms of doors did the parliamentary secretary have in mind?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There are all kinds of doors, even doors for trailers, I suppose.
It is very easy to say there are all kinds of doors. Which type of door is taxable?
A door to a cell.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I refer to a door in some moving vehicle such as a trailer, which is not intended to be covered by any item which is set forth in building materials. This is purely for clarification purposes.
Let us suppose, for example, that a board fence is built around someone's property and he puts a door in that board fence. Would that door be taxable or free?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would think that would be a gate and not a door, but if it were held to be a door then this particular section would not apply to it.

Is not the point of this change that it clarifies the situation where doors in the former schedule related to lumber and the section now does not relate to lumber, it also relates to other kinds of materials? We have a great many aluminum doors being used in ordinary buildings. Is this not the kind of situation that is attempted to be covered?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It now covers doors for buildings generally.

There are practical problems that can easily arise. I can illustrate very clearly what they are because it so happens that in my own house in Bonavista bay I have a door which I bought and put on two trestles, and it is my dining table. Would that door be taxable or not? That door was bought as building material. It so happens that it was bought with the other lumber bought to build my house, but it is not part of the building itself. It is not attached to the building and it is not used as a door.

Excise Tax Act
Is that door taxable? Am I going to have some snooper come around some day to collect 10 per cent on that door because it is not hinged to a door frame? This is the sort of thing that does arise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would have thought the hon. gentleman would have offered to pay tax in relation to that item. If it were bought for an exempt purpose, namely for use as a building material and was converted to another use, then at that stage it would become taxable. I should think the hon. member would be very willing to pay the tax at the time the change in use was entered into.

I think the hon. gentleman has contradicted himself, because at the time I bought it, according to the hon. gentleman's explanation, this door was lumber and therefore was exempt. Therefore I would not consider any tax exigible because of ex post facto legislation of this sort. I am suggesting that this legislation will create situations such as the one I have just described, and that we ought to be very clear that we are not going to create impossible administrative problems for the Department of National Revenue.
How is the lumber merchant who has to collect these taxes going to decide? How is the wholesaler going to decide at the stage at which these taxes are collected? I think the administrative problem here is much greater than the draftsmen seemed to realize when this was drafted. After all, the sales tax is not paid at the retail level. It is paid, as the hon. gentleman knows, at a much earlier stage. How is the person who pays the tax going to know, now that a member of parliament has set the fashion for the use of doors as tables, that this may not become the rage all over the country, and how is the problem going to be dealt with?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member need have no concern about it having retroactive effect, because if he will look at clause 9 of the bill he will see that the day upon which this clause comes into force is the 21st day of June, 1961. Rather than creating administrative difficulties, as the hon. member seems to fear, the belief is that this will relieve administrative difficulties. I do not think the fact that the hon. member has disclosed what he uses as his dining room table in Bonavista bay is going to create a rage for such tables across the country. I do not think the Department of National Revenue is likely to encounter any difficulty on that ground.

I am genuinely concerned about this matter. I am not in the least concerned about my dining table; I merely used

it as an example. I am genuinely concerned, however, about whether a much greater problem of enforcement is not being created than the problem the government is seeking to solve. In view of the fact that the tax is paid at the level at which it is paid by a person who cannot know what the end use is necessarily going to be, how is it going to be determined that certain of these articles which normally are for the purpose of being incorporated into buildings are not going to be so used and therefore should be taxed, and how indeed is this tax going to be collected?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This is actually a relieving section involving the widening of the present exemption. I think it must be recognized by the hon. member that the use for other purposes of doors designed primarily for buildings would be very limited indeed, and that really any problem in the administration of such other uses does not in fact arise.

Would it not be simpler just to put in the words "doors and door and window screens" and not put in this limitation with respect to use in buildings? I really do agree with the parliamentary secretary's last observation that the number of people who use doors or window screens for other purposes than for buildings is so small and the amount of tax that would be lost is so infinitesimally small that creating this distinction is simply going to create a lot of involuntary lawbreakers.
Screens are used for other purposes. As hon. members know, I was brought up on a homestead and we used screens and windows in cold frames. They were not part of a building, and surely we are not going to go around trying to collect the tiny amount of tax involved in these cases. Would it not be better to strike out "for buildings" altogether and simply say "doors and door and window screens"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The situation then would be that this clause would relate to and be dependent upon the heading "building materials". The hon. gentleman realizes that in this particular schedule we are dealing only with building materials. There are a lot of other components including vehicles and apparatus generally that have doors. It might well be said that there are forms of mouse traps that have doors.
They are not doors that are building materials.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Trains and airplanes have doors. The intention here is to make clear that these are doors for buildings so that we do not have to rely wholly upon

the simple heading of "building materials". I think the hon. member would concede that it would be bad drafting practice if one had to rely wholly upon a heading to provide the limitation within the sections which follow that particular heading.

I can see that the parliamentary secretary would have some point if the heading were not there, but obviously motor car doors or train doors would not be building materials at all, so that would explain itself. I am really quite seriously troubled by the idea of saying "doors for buildings" if it is intended to be construed as meaning doors that are used in buildings; but if it is intended to apply to every door that might be used for a building then I would not see any difficulty.
For example, from time to time I have seen doors of a certain kind used on delivery vans. They are the same kind of doors that are used in some buildings. I should think it would be the height of nonsense for the Department of National Revenue to be paying high salaries to people to go around and collect tax on the handful of doors used in the country for that sort of purpose.
If we are quite clear that what is meant by this language is doors that are capable of being used on buildings; doors that are, in other words, really building materials, and that all of them are exempt, then I would have no further quarrel, but if there is going to be some attempt made to collect the tax in the case of doors of that kind that are not actually incorporated into a building you are going to have an absolutely impossible administrative situation, and parliament should not allow these things to develop if they can be envisaged in advance. Perhaps it is not the function of an opposition to do so, but in this case I am trying to save the government from another embarrassment in addition to the many it already has.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
When the committee recessed at one o'clock the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had raised a number of questions relating to the item dealing with doors for buildings, and had suggested that perhaps we might rely entirely upon the heading of this clause for building materials. My hon. friend shakes his head, but at least that is how I interpreted the hon. gentleman's comment.
Excise Tax Act
I should like to say only that this is designed to simplify generally the administration. There are many types of doors which are not doors for buildings. The intention here, of course, is not to pursue in detail, as one could not do, those doors which are designed generally for buildings. This whole schedule has many end use items. Indeed, practically each of them is of an end use character. If one were to pursue each one to the nth degree of course it would become administratively impossible.
This amendment will enable the department to rely upon the section itself and not rely only upon the heading. In this way it will provide for administrative simplicity, as well as make it clear that it does not apply to those types of doors mentioned this morning, for mouse traps, trains and trailers, all types of doors which are not intended to be covered by the particular item under building materials.

Disregarding the reference to mouse traps, this morning reference was made to the fact that doors apply to trailers. When I occupied the position of parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance I think I exerted some influence in securing a reduction in cost to the consumers who purchased trailers. At that time we had indeed an expansionist program. At that time workers were moving across the country seeking and finding work. I refer to miners, construction, hydro workers and others. Under those circumstances it was most important, if they were to occupy temporary dwellings, that they should have the lowest possible tax impost on their housing arrangements. As one coming from northern Ontario I felt this was important.
In so far as trailers are concerned, as a result of the feeling that the consumer should be of some importance, an important reduction in the sales tax was arranged. This morning when we came to this item of doors for buildings it was a representative of the government who referred with some disdain to mobile homes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not at all.
Trailers, shall I say.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: For illustration only.

For illustration only, but I want to say that when the economy was expanding people tend to join new industries and live in what I thought was referred to disdainfully by the parliamentary secretary as trailers. Inevitably annexes are added to these trailers. A tax reduction was provided on trailers some years ago, for which I take some credit. How would the doors for these annexes now be treated? I feel that they

Excise Tax Act
would be out of court because this morning the representative of the government spoke rather assertively about trailers.
In the resource industries of this country, in the new areas of development, it has now become a practice that people bring in trailers for the purposes of having adequate dwelling places and then, as permanency is assured, they must add to the trailers and they put on annexes. As to doors and window screens with respect to such annexes as those with which I am familiar in all this new resource development area, are these items going to be denied the tax exemption? The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate very properly advanced the suggestion this morning that this defining language

and I am thinking particularly of the words "for buildings"-could perhaps be discarded. I say this because I am familiar with the kind of dwellings that have developed when there was real expansion in this economy and when people were living in trailers such as those to which the parliamentary secretary referred this morning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman is speaking of that essential and significant type of annex of which I think he is speaking, then it obviously is a building which has very high utility, and doors for such a building I think would unquestionably be exempt. The hon. gentleman has spoken of me as being disdainful of trailers. How he could have reached that conclusion I really do not know. I think it only illustrates the fact that he was grasping in some way at a straw in order to criticize this particular section of the legislation. The hon. gentleman knows, of course, that at the present time there is in the schedule an exemption which applies to trailers, and which reads as follows:
Seventy five per cent of the sale price if manufactured in Canada, or 75 per cent of the duty paid value if imported, of trailers for use as homes.
That is the existing exemption.
That is something I was influential in bringing into force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman takes the credit for that and I will not deny him the bow which he gives to himself in relation to it. I am glad that he had that influence in those days.
We are glad to know he did something.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is an old favourite of mine, so I will not pursue that matter further. I would only say to him that the type of annex to which he refers, and which has a type of door with an exterior turn knob and an interior hook, I am sure would qualify under this exemption.

I am very glad to have that assurance, Mr. Chairman, for this reason. Where there is some assurance of employment we know what happens. Everyone who experiences the movement to his constituency of these trailer camp workers knows that if there is a continuance of employment they require what I would call annexes to the custom built trailer machine and the doors that apply to it. I am glad to be assured that the doors and the window screens, if needed by these people, will have the tax exemption, although the parliamentary secretary this morning rather gave the indication that trailer people were the kind of people who had doors that would not be covered under this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the committee ready to proceed to the consideration of ducts for warm air?

No, Mr. Chairman. I think I still have a word or two to say about doors, particularly since the hon. member for Carleton has brought in the question of end use. If we could have an assurance that the government intends that all doors that are sold as building materials are going to be exempt, or that all doors that really are building materials are going to be exempt, and that there is not going to be any foolish effort to find out that a door here or there may have been used as a table or a screen here or there may have been used in a garden for a cold frame, or a window used for that purpose, I think it would be of assistance; in other words, that the wholesaler or the manufacturer from whom the tax is collected, knowing that this is a building material, will know that it is exempt from tax and will not later on have someone come and try to collect the tax because the end use was not the use that is normally given to the article. If that assurance were given I think it would not be worth while pursuing the matter any further. If the parliamentary secretary could give that kind of assurance I think it would be reassuring to those from whom the tax will be collected.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I can give my hon. friend that assurance immediately. There is certainly no intention of following each particular door. The only qualification at all that I would make is that if suddenly a rage developed, as a result of what my hon. friend said this morning, and people generally in cottages across the country were to adopt doors as a new form of dining room tables, there might have to be reconsideration of the matter. But I say to my hon. friend that there is no intention of following through at all. When a door is made ostensibly and obviously for the purpose of being incorporated into a building, then the odd case where it may be

put to some other use is not going to be followed through. If suddenly some new technique developed and it was used for other purposes, that would have to be considered and reported to parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Ducts for warm air.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary would give his explanation of this item.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, I should be glad to do so. This really adds ventilation systems to the exemption. All finished ducts for warm air and ventilation systems will hereafter be exempt from sales tax. The exemption will not apply to sheet metal or other metals or hardware which enter into the manufacture of these ducts. That is the situation at present in relation to the more limited exemption. The committee will recall that in 1960 an exemption from sales tax was provided for:
Ducts for warm air systems for heating buildings, but not including materials used in their manufacture:
Subsequently difficulty was encountered by the industry in attempting to ascertain what portion of a manufacturer's output actually qualified for the exemption. The problem arose when some ducts were incorporated in ventilation systems, in which instance they were ruled to be taxable. To differentiate between taxable and non-taxable ductsi became a troublesome and costly operation for the industry. The proposed change will do away with the problem by exempting all ducts for warm air and ventilation systems for buildings. Mr. Chairman, I resent that statement by the parliamentary secretary very much. Here is one particular law that was not in clear and simple language last year and which resulted in a misunderstanding and, as the hon. gentleman described, embarrassment for himself. He is now seeking to correct this situation by adopting other language that is not clear and simple and which is almost certainly going to result in further embarrassment.
There is one simple way to clear this whole thing up. The hon. gentleman has in front of him one of the officers from the Department of National Revenue. Let the parliamentary secretary tell us of any animal food that is taxed at the present time except those foods for laboratory animals. Surely the department knows what it is taxing, and if there is no other animal food being taxed, then there should not be a tax instituted by wording of a restrictive character. If he would drop these two adjectives so that the provision would just refer to animals, then the whole thing would be clear and there would not be any possibility of a situation arising in the next 12 months such as that which has arisen in the last 12 months. It seems to me this is a reasonable request and a simple

proposition. If food for goldfish or some other animals is being taxed, and the government still want it to be taxed, surely they know what it is, they know where the tax is being collected, and they should tell us.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is quite obvious, Mr. Chairman, to the hon. gentlemen that I have consulted with the officials who are here. So far as fur bearing or laboratory animals are concerned, they are not able to give me any exact illustration. It may be that there are some animals in zoos, I do not know. Such officials as are here are not, of course, engaged in the day to day, immediate administration of these items. This provision has been considered in some detail and, with respect, I suggest to the hon. gentlemen that there having been one, solitary representation in relation to it, they ought to be satisfied to allow the measure to pass on its present basis without further ado.

The parliamentary secretary made reference to zoos. So far as I know zoos are almost always under the jurisdiction of organizations that are non-profit organizations. Certainly, we would not want to impose a sales tax on food for animals in the zoos of this country. I think we should encourage those organizations that have this interest and encourage them to enlarge their stable in these zoos. He thought that perhaps zoos might not be exempted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said there might be; I am not in a position to tell my hon. friend. I shall be glad to get him any type of information he wishes in relation to the proposal. If my hon. friend wants to examine the problem in relation to goldfish or any of these details, I shall be glad to get him all the information in due course.

My suggestion to the parliamentary secretary was that he accept the suggestion made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and be willing to eliminate the restrictive words in this new paragraph. This new paragraph in connection with feeds for animals involve four lines of definition-too wordy. My suggestion also was that we could go on with other clauses of this bill and that the parliamentary secretary might, in due time, feel that inasmuch as there was no consequential product that would become taxable because of the restriction of the language, he might allow this clause to stand until the language is clarified. Who is interested in taxing mice, rats, hamsters, pet fish and so on? Let us not have in parliament this restriction of language, if we have intent, that would make a possibility that some of these irrelevant items might be exempt from tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

Carried.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

I wish to deal for a moment with this next item "Forest products when produced and sold by the individual settler or farmer" because I am interested in it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: May I say to the hon. gentleman that there is no change in that at all.

I wanted to ask just a question or two because I represent some farmers who sell from 1 million to 2 million or 3 million feet of lumber and timber materials a year. I want to ask whether these are exempt:	all lumber produced under these
circumstances in any quantity, timbers, pulp-wood, cordwood for stove purposes, poles, fence posts, piling, ties, cedar boughs, ornamental trees, bean poles, float logs, boom-sticks and shakebolts. I want to make certain that they all come under that classification.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has mentioned a great number of articles of the forest. All the first ones which I followed I am assured are exempt. Then I confess that I got lost with the hon. gentleman's list. I think the hon. gentleman would not wish me to give legal opinions on the floor of the House of Commons. I should be glad to get the hon. gentleman all the necessary information. Indeed I think most of the items he has mentioned, if not all of them, are exempt. With such a long list it is very difficult to follow them all.

I wish to point out that they are all forest products produced and sold by individual settlers or farmers in my constituency. Every one of the items I have mentioned is in that category. I just asked the question:	Do they come under this
clause? They are all forest products, every one of them. I mentioned cedar boughs, for instance.

for ornamental purposes. As to bean poles, there is quite a market for them now, for stringer beans, scarlet runners and things of that kind. Then there are float logs; they are cedar logs supplied for holding up floats on which machinery is placed. Then there are boomsticks. Boomsticks are logs supplied for forming bag booms.
Such as they have on the Ottawa river.

Then there are shakebolts. They are split sections of cedar logs averaging from two feet to three feet in length from which shakes are later split or sawn. However, they are forest products. I mention the matter because this was brought to my attention and some question was raised about this clause. Then there are railroad ties. I think we are fairly certain of the more or less stable products. However, there are some products here that are not manufactured or not sold generally by farmers from their woodlots and so on, but these products are all sold by settlers or farmers in my constituency off the forested portion of their properties.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
May I say first that there has been no amendment to this particular section, and I do not know whether we are in order in discussing it. The general heading is "Forest products when produced and sold by the individual settler or farmer". The hon. gentleman can interpret that as well as I can. He then mentions a long list of items. Some of them are not produced in my constituency. I am not familiar with them. I would not wish on the floor of the House of Commons to seek to give an opinion in respect of the tax status of each of those items. If they come within the generic heading "Forest products when produced and sold by the individual settler or farmer", then obviously they are tax exempt.
I am sure the hon. gentleman will be fair enough to realize that when he mentions a particular type of forest product with which I am not familiar, it will perhaps be difficult for me to give him a specific answer in relation to it. From listening to the list, so far as I can see I would say the products he mentions probably are all exempt. However, I should be glad to make a detailed inquiry on his behalf, particularly in view of the fact that this item is not being amended by the proposed legislation.

I wish the parliamentary secretary would do that. I can assure him that they are all forest products and that

Excise Tax Act
they are all produced by settlers or individual farmers. I wanted to be quite certain about one or two of them which are rather unusual.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
We now turn to page 7, "Preparations, chemicals or poisons".

Mr. Chairman, could the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) tell the house if chemicals used in the production of poisons for pest control purposes in agriculture or horticulture are exempt from excise tax? Could he also tell us if the materials that are used in the production of poisons against small animals such as rats and field mice that gnaw fruit trees in winter are exempt from that same tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

I asked the question because the text is not clear. In fact, it reads as follows:
-for pest control purposes-
Can we consider small animals like rats and field mice as pests? If I understand correctly, a pest-
You know what a pest is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have not the French text in front of me. In the English version the language is "poisons for pest control". That certainly would clearly cover what the hon. member has in mind. I would think that the word "parasite", en frangais, would cover it as well.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The next item for consideration is-
The parliamentary secretary has not told us how much of this is really new.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This paragraph clarifies the existing exemption for and I quote:
Preparations, chemicals or poisons for pest control purposes in agriculture or horticulture and materials for use exclusively in the manufacture thereof.
This exemption was intended as a relief for the farmer by providing an exemption for poisons and insecticides. Recently the manufacturers have claimed that it is applicable to a number of pharmaceuticals on the

ground that their use in treating skin diseases and internal disorders caused by bacteria, internal parasites and similar infections is, in fact, the control of a pest. This interpretation would broaden the existing exemption beyond what was originally intended and would also exempt drugs and medicines which are taxable when used in the treatment of human and animal diseases. The particular amendment is for the purpose of clarification and assuring that it conforms with what was the original intention of parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The next item, as I was pointing out, is "Self-propelled, selfunloading forage wagons". Is there any explanation on the part of the parliamentary secretary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This covers a reasonably newly designed item of farm machinery and adds that to farm machinery exemption. It exempts a self-propelled wagon fitted with a mechanical device for unloading. The use of the equipment of course, as hon. gentlemen realize, speeds up the operation of transporting forage from the field and unloading it in a storage location. These vehicles have not been produced in Canada to any extent until quite recently.
Generally items of farm machinery are exempt from sales tax. They are covered by the wording of tariff items 409 and 409a and some other items which are listed in schedule III of the Excise Tax Act. However these particular forage wagons did not qualify under the wording of the tariff item and special mention is made in schedule III to make them exempt. It is very difficult to determine what the result of the exemption may be upon the revenue. It is probably not large, but it could be considerable if the popularity of these vehicles grows. (Translation):

Will the exemption from excise tax on this machinery result in an increase in the price of milk? As you know, in the past three years, the price of milk has come down 40 or 45 cents per hundred pounds.
(Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I confess I am unable to relate what the hon. gentleman says, dealing with the price of milk, to the sales tax exemption on forage wagons. This sales tax exemption will reduce the cost of production for farmers, and by reducing the cost of production for farmers it will, I hope, enable them to make a larger profit. I think it has nothing to do with what the selling price of milk may be.

In subclause 3 of clause 8 of this bill we are dealing with items under the heading "farm and forest". In the budget

presented by the Minister of Finance, on the tariff side-and we have not had an opportunity to come to that yet-there are porposals which in the opinion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture will increase the cost of production in agriculture, about which the parliamentary secretary just mentioned. I refer to the increase in tariff protection on nails.
In so far as the "farm and forest" schedule is concerned, belatedly referring it back to subclause 1 "building materials", what is the consistency in the proposals advanced now, relating sales tax to tariff? What is the consistency of certain reductions in schedule III under the heading "farm and forest" in relation to our discussion on certain items of reduction under the schedule "building materials" in subclause 1?
Would the parliamentary secretary explain to the committee, so that we may explain it to the farming community and answer the brief presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, why on the other side of the tax field, the tariff side, after this budget, it is likely that for instance the cost of nails to the farmer will increase? What is the relationship between reductions under this "farm and forest" schedule and the other side of the budget picture which, in the opinion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, involves farmers in increased costs because of an increase in the price of nails?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I understand the hon. gentleman's comment it is that in another bill there is an increase in tariff. The hon. gentleman wants me to reconcile an increase in tariff on nails with the elimination of sales tax on self-propelled forage wagons.
No, on the whole of subsection 3.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is giving me a rather considerable task in asking me to reconcile those matters, which in my submission to the committee do not really relate. When we come to the question of the Customs Tariff and the item dealing with nails I will be glad to discuss that matter with the hon. gentleman, or the minister will be glad to discuss it with him, and I believe will satisfy him that the action proposed in respect of nails is one which is to the advantage of all Canadians, the producers of nails and the consumers of nails alike. I think at this stage, when we are dealing with self-propelled forage wagons, that is about all I can say.

I was not, of course, directing my comment to the item related to self-propelled forage wagons, preparations,
Excise Tax Act
chemicals, or feeds for poultry. I was referring to the heading of the subsection, which covers sales tax benefits or otherwise that are available to farm and forest people.
I simply thought it appropriate at this stage to ask the parliamentary secretary about the other side of the budget picture, when under another bill that will come before us, perhaps tomorrow, added protection will be given to the manufacturers of nails which has been protested by the farming community. I thought it quite appropriate, when we are dealing with certain eliminations of sales tax in the farm and forest field, to ask how this will compensate in dollars and cents value the farming community in relation to an impost they expect as a result of the tarif increase on nails.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The whole situation with respect to nails will be dealt with in the committee when we reach the Customs Tariff. I will be glad to discuss the matter with the hon. gentleman at that time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall we now proceed to the item dealing with additives for fuel oil for heating, etc.?

Mr. Chairman, before we go to the particular items under that heading of "miscellaneous" I should like for a moment to express the disappointment I think is felt by everyone connected with the fishing industry because of the omission of certain tax relief they have been seeking in order to put the fishing industry on a somewhat comparable basis with other primary industries in the country.
The minister received representations from the Fisheries Council of Canada long before the budget with respect to certain changes they hoped would be made in the sales tax in this particular legislation. There was, as the minister well knows, a change made in 1939 with regard to diesel fuel supplied to draggers and trawlers measuring at least 45 feet in length and licensed by the Department of Fisheries. It is very difficult for those engaged in the fishing industry to understand why the fuel oil used by fishermen who can afford a boat measuring 45 feet or longer should be exempt from sales tax and it should not be the case with smaller boats.
There was a great hope that the fishermen of these smaller boats which cannot make a five-day voyage would be treated on the same basis as fishermen with larger vessels. I cannot find anything in the language here that would suggest this change has been made.
I am not an expert on this matter but just want to be sure that this request has been refused. I would be even happier if told that I am not reading the bill carefully enough

Excise Tax Act
and that in fact it has been done. If that is the case, I will sit down at once and allow the parliamentary secretary to tell me so.
There was also representation made that the excise tax on diesel fuel oil used in internal combustion engines to generate electricity for commercial fishing industries should be dropped, as has been the case in regard to certain other primary industries. Again I make the same remark in that regard; if by any chance I have not found the change and it is here, I would be very happy indeed to hear about it. If there is no change in that regard then I must express regret that it has not been changed. This was done in respect to the logging and mining industries and it is very hard for fishermen to understand why they should not be treated in the same way. I am sure the parliamentary secretary can understand that feeling.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He is very anxious to go fishing anyway.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The parliamentary secretary is very anxious to go fishing.

The parliamentary secretary is no more anxious to go fishing than the member for Bonavista-Twillingate is anxious to go to the fishing parts of this country instead of sitting here. I should like to be able to go and tell the fishermen that the government at long last has met some of the requests of the fishing industry. If it has I do not want to waste the time of the committee, but if it has not I want to make a plea that in the next budget, if we are ever to have another budget from this government-
You will not.
-the government should do just what it has failed to do this year, that is, to pay some attention to the representations received from the fisheries council.

They will not have
another chance. This is their last chance.

This is something that is not of very great interest to the fishing industries in my constituency and perhaps in any part of Newfoundland, but it is of importance to certain northern fisheries in which an hon. member accused me the other day of taking no interest at a time when we were debating the Pine Point railway, which is apparently another vision like the Columbia river, according to what we were told this morning. The fisheries council asked that the sales and excise taxes be removed from certain vehicles such as snowmobiles and track type vehicles for use in respect of the northern

fisheries in the wintertime. I cannot find in this bill any indication that this change has been made, but I would be very glad if told that this has been done. If it has not been done 1 hope if there is another budget presented by this government that consideration will be given to this change.
I know that the parliamentary secretary does not like any reference to nails.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Only on appropriate occasions.

I suggest this is an appropriate occasion. According to the brief presented by the Fisheries Council of Canada nails are plentifully used in the construction of sardine weirs and lobster traps and, therefore, a request was made that nails for this purpose should also be exempted from tax. It does seem to me that the time has arrived when some attention should be given to these requests of the fisheries council. I take this opportunity to record those requests and to say that I hope they will not be ignored much longer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the particular section with which we are now dealing has reference to only two matters, additives to fuel oil and seismic shot hole casings, and does not deal with the matters to which the hon. gentleman has referred. Those matters are not new matters. I believe they have been referred to governments for some period of time, and I have no doubt that when my hon. friend occupied a position on the treasury benches representations in respect to these matters were made to him.

I can assure the hon. gentleman that they were not, because at that time there was no exemption in respect of diesel fuel used by the lumber and mining industries, and it is only because of this exemption to the lumber and mining industries that the fishermen find it impossible to understand why they are not to be treated equally. This is a matter that has arisen since the present government came into office.
In respect to the question regarding this northern equipment, I am not able to say for sure whether representations were made five years ago, but I would be very doubtful that they were. There has been great development each year in the kind of machinery used for this purpose.
Regarding the other questions, I am not sure there was ever any such representation made before, but I would be very surprised to find that there was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
From what the hon. gentleman said earlier he realizes there is a

very serious end use problem in relation to some of the matters he has raised.

I am very well aware of that fact, but hope that the hon. gentleman is not insinuating that fishermen, if they had a tax exemption, would use diesel oil to go on holidays, because the average fisherman operating a small vessel must work all the time during the fishing season to make a living and does not have the opportunity of taking a pleasure cruise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I make no insinuations at all.

Mr. Chairman, we are dealing with a clause of the excise tax bill which is headed "Miscellaneous". We in the opposition do not receive regularly all the representations which are made to the government, in the course of a year, prior to its presentation of a budget. I should like the parliamentary secretary to tell us whether the government has received representations throughout the year and what decisions have been made in this regard. I can find nothing included in this bill changing the sales tax in respect to margarine, and should like to know the reason why this has not been changed.
I should also like to ask the parliamentary secretary whether or not representations have been received during the year from soft drink manufacturers regarding the elimination of sales tax on their products and, if so, I should like to know why those representations have not caused this administration to revise the law in this respect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has dealt with two hardy perennial matters. The first deals with margarine and, as the hon. gentleman has said, there is no change in this bill in that regard. I was interested in noting that the hon. gentleman apparently advocated the elimination of sales tax on margarine and trust he was speaking in that respect for his party.
I did not say that at all. I asked for information in regard to whether the government had received representations of this kind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman knows, during the years he was parliamentary secretary representations were received in this regard and they continue to be received.

Representations also have been received in regard to the sales tax on soft drinks but the decision is as indicated in the bill before the committee.

No action.
(Translation) :
Are we now on item 4, page 7 of the English version?

speechtext:
We are now on the fuel
oil item.
(Text):

I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary why this has been limited to drain tile not exceeding four inches, because many farmers use much larger tiles in the construction of culverts, and would appreciate an exemption of tax in that regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In respect of this item, Mr. Chairman, there is no change. It will be remembered that I dealt with the matter before the committee last year. My recollection is that there is another item. Drain tiles for agricultural purposes are exempt whatever their diameter may be.
What page is that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is page 30 of the consolidation of August, 1960 of the Excise Tax Act.
Since last year-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think it has an earlier history. I was informed on this when it was before the committee last year. Because this is not a new item I have not informed myself this year. I cannot give the hon. gentleman the exact date. I shall be glad to look into it and write my hon. friend.
Last year, or it may be two years ago, I was in contact with a farmer who paid a tax on tile especially for drainage. I made representations at that time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think this goes back to an earlier date than that but I would have to look into the details.
Some time prior to the 1957 revision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think it goes back quite a little time. "Drain tile for agricultural purposes" as an exemption goes back quite a few years.

The hon. member raises quite an important point. I have had questions about this from my own riding. I refer the parliamentary secretary to the bill before us. This, of course, refers to present law. In subparagraph (3) he will find reference

Excise Tax Act
to drain tiles for agricultural purposes. When we come to consider subparagraph (4) on page 7 of the bill before us we shall see a reference to drain tiles not exceeding four inches in inside diameter and 12 inches in length. Perhaps at a convenient time the parliamentary secretary would explain to the hon. member who raised this question the difference between the exemption in one subparagraph and the other.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If they are drain tile for agricultural purposes they are exempt whatever their diameter and whatever their length. If they are for other purposes, then they are exempt only if they do not exceed four inches in inside diameter and 12 inches in length.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed with the next item having to do with seismic shot-hole casing and materials used in the manufacture thereof?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I confess that until this was raised I did not know what a seismic shot-hole casing was. It is something that is used in tests to register vibration waves from underground explosions set off to determine the nature of subsoil geological formations in locations where oil and gas reserves are likely to be found. Recently a Canadian manufacturer commenced manufacturing these casings out of wax saturated paper.
This product competes with similar imported articles of steel which are not subject to sales tax as they enter Canada under tariff item 399a or 848, enumerated in schedule III to the Excise Tax Act. Under existing legislation, the Canadian product is subject to sales tax while the imported article is exempt from the levy. The proposed amendment will rectify the situation by making all seismic shot-hole casing and the materials used in its manufacture exempt from sales tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we proceed with the next item having to do with laminated timber for bridges which is to be found on page 8 of the bill?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is simply to provide for equal treatment between the various types of materials which are used in bridges.
Municipalities are exempt from sales tax on their purchases of structural steel and aluminum for bridges and precast concrete shapes for bridges in public highway systems. However, sawn and glued laminated timber which is often used in bridge construction as a material alternative to structural steel and

aluminum has been held to be taxable. From a competitive point of view, sawn and glued laminated timber is just as strong and durable as structural steel and aluminum, or so I am advised, and it is said to offer the advantage of lower maintenance costs. It would appear that a number of municipalities have shown interest in using it instead of its metal counterparts.
The exemption of laminated timber purchased by municipalities for incorporation in bridge structures would put this product on the same sales tax basis as its competitors, aluminum and steel. Moreover the materials entering into the manufacture of laminated timber such as glue and other required chemicals will also be exempt.

We are dealing here in a broad way, Mr. Chairman, with the portion of schedule III of the act which refers to exemptions of sales tax for municipalities. I recall very vividly that when the Minister of Finance was in opposition he was a very strong spokesman for the idea that all the goods sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale should not be subject to federal sales tax. Under the present regime we have had very few exemptions. Indeed, we have had increases in the over-all sales tax. It has gone from 10 per cent to 11 per cent on the items that are not covered here, and some others. Before we pass this paragraph we should hear from the spokesmen for the administration about their present views with respect to the propriety of taxing goods sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale and in particular when a greater impost is involved today on some items than was the case in 1956 and 1957, when the Minister of Finance and others had so much to say about the injustice of taxing items purchased by municipalities and school boards which were subject to federal sales tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have already dealt with the only item which is actually changed in this particular schedule; but the hon. member is, of course, well aware of the rather substantial number of items which have been changed since 1957. The Minister of Finance has been responsible for the inclusion in this particular schedule of a large number of items which have meant a great deal to municipalities across Canada.

But the Minister of
Finance said none of them should be subject to tax.
