speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the house was good enough to permit me to offer a word of explanation of this particular item on Saturday morning. The explanation is to be found at page 7352 of Hansard. In the budget speech I made reference to the fact that there were negotiations pending under the provisions of GATT with respect to sodium hypochlorite laundry bleach and I hoped that the negotiations might be concluded prior to the passage of the resolutions in the committee of ways and means. Actually the resolutions were reported out of the committee at noon on Friday. On Friday afternoon I received a message from Mr. Hector McKinnon, who has been conducting negotiations with the representatives of the United States at Geneva on this subject, that he had arrived at a package deal. It is contained in the amendment now put forward and which is to be found on page 4 of Votes and Proceedings of June 30.
In effect we are proposing three temporary items. The committee is aware that at the present time the tariff board is conducting under a reference a review of all the items in the Customs Tariff pertaining to chemicals. It was thought desirable that, pending this review of the entire chemical section of the tariff, the rates that have been applicable to sodium hypochlorite hitherto according to 90205-6-469
Customs Tariff
the general understanding should continue. However, we observe that there are three items involved here. As I say, these represent a package agreement with the United States in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to make a very few observations with regard to the fishing industry on the second reading of this bill along lines similar to those I made in committee on the excise tax bill and to draw attention to the recommendations that were made to the minister on February 16 by the Fisheries Council of Canada. I have a copy of their letter in my hand at the present time. I should like to save the time of the committee by reading certain sections of this letter and by making their requests my own.

Customs Tariff
The fisheries council points out that the fishing industry derives two thirds of its income from sales made in the export market. Indeed, so far as I know there is no industry that depends more for its prosperity on the export market than the fishing industry does. One half of its total income is derived from sales in the United States. This really gives emphasis to two points, first, that the industry must sell on world markets in competition with other large fish producing nations and, second, that in the fishery we are very dependent on the United States market.
Then the letter goes on to point out how increasingly difficult it is in that industry to compete with countries such as Iceland, France, Norway, Denmark, Japan and Peru which have lower standards of living and where the degree of subsidization of the fishing industry exceeds anything ever thought of in Canada. This is simply to emphasize the fact that the fishing industry, if it is to survive at all much less provide a decent income for those engaged in it, has to be competitive. It is true also that the costs, as the fisheries council points out, have been advancing faster than the prices received for the product. That is not true in every case but in most cases.
One of the difficulties is that there has been inability to modernize the fleet, particularly on the east coast, and notwithstanding the announcements made repeatedly by the government they still have not brought forward their regulations for the aid they propose to give in this field. I am not going into the problems we have with competition right in our own waters because this is not really strictly relevant.
I go on from there to the budget proposals that were made to the minister so far as the Customs Tariff is concerned. I have already said something about those so far as excise tax is concerned. I should like to run over them briefly. The first was with respect to tariff item 682 which provides for the free entry of fishing nets and nets of all kinds. This is an item which is bound under GATT and the fisheries council was disturbed that there might be some attempt made to impose a tariff in this respect. However, I understand that fear was not in fact realized, I am happy to say.
Then, they went on to make representations with respect to some items that had a duty that should not have a duty. I want to say in general terms at this point that it does seem to me the time has come when the fishing industry should be put on a genuine basis of equality with the farm industry in respect of its instruments of production. This ought to be our goal. I come to these particular items.
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
One was trawl doors. I am not going into the details of them. Another item was inflatable life rafts and a third was aluminum fishboxes and pen boards. It seems to me that, in view of the importance of these items in the export industry, there was a very good case for giving consideration to them.
Under tariff item 418, they ask that certain changes should be made in respect of machinery and apparatus and parts thereof for use exclusively in the manufacture of fishmeal, liquid fish and fish solubles, stock and poultry food and fertilizers from fish and waste products thereof. They endorse certain suggestions for negotiations under GATT in this regard.
The next item was a proposal for a change in item 21 lx. Then there was another suggestion with respect to vessels, item 439g. There was another in respect of cordage in combination with metal strands; another with respect to recording paper. I am not going to take the time of the committee to read these. There was another very important one with respect to salt fish driers. I may say that there is nothing more important than getting the cost of salt fish driers down to the lowest possible figure because our whole competitive position in the salt fish market depends on getting the cost of our product down to a competitive level with other producers.
I have in my hand a bulletin of the Fisheries Council of Canada, which appeared on June 26. The fisheries council was very disappointed in the budget so far as the Customs Tariff was concerned. They said that action taken in respect of the duty on anchors ignored the advice of the council. It should be made clear that the duty would not apply to commercial fishermen. In future there will be a 15 per cent duty applied on all anchors of less than 40 pounds in weight from the commonwealth or most favoured nation countries. Those weighing 40 pounds or more will continue to come in duty free. Surely, this government is not so much in need of revenue that it has to apply a duty on small anchors.
Then, of course, there was the admission of live trout for commercial trout farms. The council was pleased with that but it is not going to help the fishing industry generally very much. Machinery for use in making nets or netting is placed on the free list from most favoured nation countries, a reduction from a 5 per cent rate, for which they were glad. They said these were the only tariff changes of any direct interest to the fishing industry. I do feel, sir, that anyone who like me represents a community that is dependent on the fishing industry for its livelihood, is justified in expressing the disappointment

that the fishing industry is not treated in the same way that the farmers are treated in respect of taxes.

Mr. Chairman, I hope I shall always be frank with the committee. I made explicit reference to the matter in the budget speech on June 20, so that there has been opportunity for anyone interested in the item to make representations in the light of the statement I made in the budget speech. But one thing that was not completed at the time of the budget speech was the GATT negotiations. I gave the house a full report at the time on the course of the negotiations, and last Saturday I reported the conclusion of the negotiations and the terms of the agreement reached.
As I mentioned earlier, Mr. Chairman, this all arises out of a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada which involved the classification under a particular item of the Canadian tariff of sodium hypochlorite in solution. The decision of the supreme court turned on the classification. The result of the decision was to upset the departmental rulings of recent years on this commodity. This would involve jobs for a good many Canadians. We felt that the present terms of tariff entry of sodium hypochlorite in solution were fair and reasonable; that is to say, 15 per cent B.P. and 20 per cent m.f.n. We thought it was most regrettable also that this change which denied to our Canadian producers the protection under which they had carried on business for years should be suddenly withdrawn while the whole question was before the tariff board. Therefore the action that we proposed was one that would reinstate the tariff protection but not indefinitely; to put a time limit on it, as we have done in this amendment, so that the whole question can be reviewed at a time when we can be reasonably confident that we will have received the report of the tariff board.
We then set to work to negotiate with the countries concerned. Following extensive negotiations carried on at Geneva by Mr. Hector McKinnon, who is leading the Canadian team in the current GATT negotiations there, and who commands so much esteem and respect on the part of hon. members in all parts of the house, we arrived only last Friday at the agreement. I mentioned the wire from Mr. McKinnon announcing the agreement arrived on Friday afternoon. Therefore we moved just as swiftly as it was possible to do. I put the notice of motion on Votes and Proceedings that afternoon.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, we have had extensive requests for the reinstatement of the rates. Firms and associations that made representations requesting the former rate be reinstated are quite numerous.

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-117, to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few very brief remarks to make on this bill. The principle of the bill is to extend the definition of industrial enterprise or, in other words, to extend effectively the authority of the industrial development bank by permitting it to lend to any industry whereas formerly the bank was limited with regard to those classes of industry it could assist. There are other consequential amendments and there is an increase in the amount of money available for lending.
I think all hon. members will agree that it is desirable that the jurisdiction and authority of the bank should be extended. There is no quarrel with that purpose. What concerns me is that the principle involves not merely the extension of the authority of the bank to lend but goes so far as to permit the bank to lend to a business or undertaking of any kind. In other words, there are the widest possible ramifications.
In the final analysis the industrial development bank is using the taxpayers' money to lend to business. The bank has a good record and over the years has done a great deal for the economy of the country. But I for one cannot let second reading pass without expressing my displeasure at the way the principle of extending the activity of the bank is being carried out by the government. For instance, speaking only for myself I cannot accept without a word of protest the principle that the taxpayers' money should be gathered by the taxing authorities and made available through the industrial development bank for lending to any business whatever.
When taxation is bearing so heavily on our people, as it is and of necessity must with our expenditures at such a high level, surely it is not proper that money taken from the taxpayers should be used for lending to any business whatever. It is the principle arising out of the use of that very broad word any that causes me difficulty.
I know it is a bad thing in arguing on a matter of principle to use particular references. It is a poor way to argue but perhaps it does have the merit of bringing attention to the point at issue. Surely our taxpayers are not to be taxed, for instance, for the purpose of making 'heir money available by way of 90205-6-470
3, 1961
Industrial Development Bank Act loans for the development of race tracks, however pleasant these places may be to a great many of us. Surely that is not a desirable principle, and yet that is exactly what is being done by this kind of legislation. Surely it is not desirable that the taxpayers' money should be lent to certain limited types of amusement places which do not meet the requirements of most taxpayers in this country. I could go on and drag in other examples that would probably make the legislation look a little ridiculous in this context. However, I will content myself with illustrating the point as I have and expressing my regret that the government saw fit to use this particular method in the desirable extension of authority under the act. Surely the principle could have been carried out in a better way, in a manner that would more accurately express the wishes of the Canadian people, because it seems to me that this way completely ignores the rights of the taxpayers who are providing the funds.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on second reading of the bill may I say that I think there is one point which has not been brought to the attention of the house even though I am sure all hon. members realize it. The president of the industrial development bank is the same Mr. Coyne who has created quite a furor around the house in the last number of weeks. Mr. Coyne is the president of the bank and evidently the government is very happy with the way that the bank has been operated. Evidently Mr. Coyne's policies have been very highly suspect in other areas but so far as the industrial development bank is concerned everything seems to be going fine.
Quite frankly, before the bill comes to a vote I should like to know just what the relationship has been between the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the president of the industrial development bank. We know what the relationship has been between the Minister of Finance and the president of the Bank of Canada, but before a measure like this is passed surely we should know whether the president is in agreement with these particular provisions and whether the board of directors was brought into this whole field. In view of the rather astounding revelations which have taken place with regard to the other position of Mr. Coyne over the last number of months, I really wonder exactly what his position would be as president of this particular institution in which we are making such a very great change.
For example, Mr. Coyne has been called restrictionist. As president of the industrial development bank he has increased the amount of money lent by 26 per cent and the

Industrial Development Bank Act number of loans by 24 per cent. It is rather interesting to note that the bank lending rate went from 6J per cent to 7 per cent in September, 1959, and was brought down to 6J per cent again by September 1960. It would seem that the president of the industrial development bank is following the suggestion of the Minister of Finance about lowering interest rates.
He is leading.

It appears to me that it is the president of the Bank of Canada who seems to be getting into all the trouble. In the remarks which the minister made to the house he referred to the full support of the government. Evidently the president of the industrial development bank has the full support of the government. The bank has expanded its operations considerably over the past few years. I assume these are the activities of the same Mr. Coyne. The borrowing authority has been extended from three times the aggregate of capital plus reserve funds to five times the aggregate and it would seem that this is the old easy money policy. I should like to know whether Mr. Coyne concurred in this. If he did, certainly here is easy money. Here are the expansionist theories of the Minister of Finance and the government right in the one area where Mr. Coyne reigns supreme. When the minister spoke at the resolution stage he said, as found at page 7312 of Hansard:
-it is the hope of the government that in this way the industrial development bank can also contribute to the retention in Canada of the ownership and control of Canadian businesses.
Mr. Coyne has been wandering right across the country suggesting this and yet the Minister of Finance puts forward the fact that the industrial development bank is going to put Mr. Coyne's views into action by providing opportunities for Canadian businessmen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Those views are not indigenous to Mr. Coyne alone.
I am sorry, I did not hear that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Those views do not entirely belong to Mr. Coyne alone.

These were certainly some of the main points Mr. Coyne was making in his speeches and it was evidently his speeches which were causing a great deal of embarrassment to the government. We can only assume that some of these ideas were the ones which brought about the concern of the men on the treasury benches. I do not like to open the hatch to a debate on Mr. Coyne, especially when we are going to hear a great deal about him tomorrow. Nevertheless, I think there are some interesting aspects to

this whole business when we realize that we are going about the process of extending the scope of the industrial development bank. We are in the process of extending the amount of money the bank would have to lend under a president whom we have been told is completely incompetent. I feel this is rather disturbing. Is Mr. Coyne going to remain as president of the industrial development bank? In the annual report, he is listed as president, not because he is president of the Bank of Canada but simply because he is president. I rather suspect he is president of the industrial development bank because he is president of the Bank of Canada.
The office of president of the industrial development bank is not included in the legislation which we are going to be reviewing once again tomorrow. I feel this is a matter of great interest in connection with the bill now before us. We should have a full explanation as to what the position is in regard to Mr. Coyne, not as president of the Bank of Canada but as president of the industrial development bank. It would seem to me that the confidence of the business community is at stake. Certainly, I should like to know whether or not the board of directors and the president of the industrial development bank were made aware of the government's scheme. We are told that Mr. Coyne did not even know what was in the budget until he opened his newspaper the next morning, at which time evidently he was at Stratford.
We have before us a bill to change an enterprise under the jurisdiction of a man who does not even know what is going to happen to that enterprise. Has he been told how the scope of the bank is going to be extended? I think the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) had a very good point. I wonder what Mr. Coyne would say? He has been the head of the organization for six and a half years and he must know something about the activities of this bank, where its weaknesses lie, and so on. We understand from the minister that Mr. Coyne knew nothing of what was in the budget. Presumably, he did not know what was going to happen to the industrial development bank either. While we are discussing this bill during the next few minutes I hope we will hear about Mr. Coyne, not so much as president of the Bank of Canada but as president of the industrial development bank.

I rise just briefly, Mr. Speaker, to express our support of this measure because, in our opinion, it is an extension of the use of social capital for the development of this country and its

enterprises. I suppose that basically the purpose of the bill is to extend the definition of industrial enterprise to include an industry, trade or business of any kind. I am pleased to see this amendment proposed. Personally, 1 have had some knowledge, from a local point of view, of the application or administration of the industrial development bank and the purpose it has served, particularly in the forest industry in the area which 1 have the honour to represent.
For a considerable time, Mr. Speaker, I have considered it was somewhat limited in its scope and opportunities for making loans or various grants to industries or businesses. I have been under the impression that the larger companies, on the whole, have been best able to take advantage of this legislation. I trust that the amendments contained in this bill will mean that the bank will have an opportunity in the future to assist to a greater extent than in the past the medium and small sized businesses in the country.
I am pleased also to note the increase in capital to $50 million, and consequently the increase that can be made in aggregate loans, investments, guarantees and other liabilities. In considering this bill, I am somewhat inclined to be parochial in my approach. I can see great opportunities for the, shall I say, very sound application of the terms of this bill to the district which I have the honour to represent, to a number of industries and businesses that have been denied that opportunity to date. I am thinking particularly of the development of tourist resorts and places that provide recreational facilities, things of that type. When the minister replies, I should like him to give us a little more information in that connection. Will these amendments make it possible to assist that type of industry or business, whatever you like to call it?
In conclusion, let me say that I believe this is a progressive step and we support it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of these amendments and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I have been interested in this subject for some time. When the minister introduced the resolution last Friday, as recorded at page 7310 of Hansard, he gave a full explanation of this measure. I would hope, unlike the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith), that this bill would not take too long to pass.
The question that arises in my mind is, is this the answer to many of our problems? Will it go far enough? I should like to quote a part of the resolution which introduced this measure:
90205-6-470i
3, 1961
Industrial Development Bank Act That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act to enlarge the classes of loans that may be made under the act so as to include therein all business enterprises without limitation as to the kind of business carried on.
Now, in analysing that part of the resolution, I should think that this would empower the bank to take at least a calculated risk in connection with applications that envisage, for instance, the development of our resources and which would help our unemployment problem. In addition, this measure would aid Canadian control of companies. For instance, I have one company in mind that is very dear to my heart, the Alberta Pulp Mill. This company is composed of 46 sound businessmen who have spent upwards of $200,000 in making surveys on the ground and from the air of certain timber limits. They have made application and will get a licence for 6,000 square miles of a species of white spruce which they tell me will compare with that in any area on the North American continent. At the moment, this company is at the stage where it needs from $150,000 to $200,000 to get a feasibility report. This money is available in the United States but it does mean losing Canadian control. There may be some risk involved, but I think it is a calculated risk.
On the other hand, there have been three feasibility reports made in this area by the same engineers, and they tell me that this particular area is better than either of the others. I hope that these amendments will provide a means for developing our own resources so that Canadians will be employed and Canadian control of the companies will be maintained. I think that this is something that we must foster, for the reason that I think we are lacking in this respect. If we ever want to attract Canadian money into our own resources, I think this is setting a pattern that can be followed.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday when the resolution was before us the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicated that we in this party would certainly have no objection to this legislation. Indeed we have advocated this type of thing for some time. In my remarks in connection with the budget I mentioned that, if we had in this country an expansionist government, I was surprised that in the legislative program announced last November there was no reference to expanding in this desirable field.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat, namely the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Rogers) asked the question: Will this bill go far enough? That is indeed an interesting question. It relates to the expansionist

Industrial Development Bank Act idea that this administration may have had at the time they asked us to assemble here last November and the fact that we find nine months later that something as important as this only now comes before us. What has happened in this cabinet which is supposed to be a cabinet that had some vision and some expansionist tendencies as outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) so recently? Rumours have been going around that they had done some thinking along the lines of expansion beyond what is presented to us in this bill. I refer to a date as far back as February 18, 1961, when the Financial Post contained an article under the heading "Ottawa Studies Plan to Lend Risk Capital".
From its Ottawa staff, the Financial Post surmised that specific proposals for setting up a new $1 billion national development corporation which could supply risk capital for Canadian ventures were before the cabinet. What has happened to that proposal in an expansionist government referred to by the Minister of Finance just prior to the introduction of his budget? This article went on to say that it was believed that this corporation to be sponsored by the government would be intended to take a far more aggressive role than the industrial development bank, a federal agency established in 1944 to fill what appeared to be a gap in the existing financial machinery of this country, according to official descriptions of its position. Is this not a puny effort if this proposal was considered by an expansionist government in February as suggested by this article?
To indicate that it was not only one of our friends in the press gallery who had heard of this activity, I refer to another. I refer to an article of Mr. Peter Dempson of the Toronto Telegram which is not unfriendly to the present administration. His report dated May 25, prior to the budget, states this:
One of the main provisions in the budget will be the financing of a national development fund, designed to stimulate the economy and create jobs. Reports have suggested the fund may run from $500 million to $1 billion.
We have the result. We have this bill. This advancement in the role of the industrial development bank, is of course, approved on this side. It is in accord with a resolution of this party presented in January at our national rally. It does not go as far as we suggested in our resolution at that time. However, it is significant that the government did not have it in mind when they proposed legislation for this session last November. It is also significant that it appears to be in the Coyne budget presented to the Minister of Finance last February, although some of the items in the Coyne budget are not acceptable to those of us on this side. However, what

surprises me is this, and I hope that the minister, when he replies, will give us information on this point. We are increasing-and I say we agree to increase it-the capital of the industrial development bank. But what is the obligation with respect to non-budgetary transactions and net cash requirements of the government for the current fiscal year as a result of this decision? At page 6666 of Hansard I note in the budget speech of the minister a reference to his cash requirements. Hon. members will recollect that it was a cash requirement beyond the budgetary items of $1 billion.

It was a cash requirement including the deficit of $1 billion. There was, of course, this interesting dash. There is just an item of a dash in connection with exchange fund liabilities; no figure is given for that item. But regardless of that, I find nothing here that relates to the supply of capital, either on a budgetary basis or a cash basis, during the fiscal year for the industrial development bank and its proposed expansion which would be in accord with the bill before us.
I ask the minister to tell us something about that matter. Is this going to be printing press money that supplies the capital that will be available under the terms of this statute or in what way is this to be financed through the Bank of Canada? It is known to this house that, at our rally and following the rally in January of this year, this party took the position that the industrial development bank should be separated from the Bank of Canada. I find here that in the bill-and of course, we shall discuss the individual clauses later

there is a continuation of the stipulation that the executive committee of the bank will be those persons who happen to belong to the executive committee of the Bank of Canada. I hope that hon. members of the house will seriously consider whether that is a desirable feature which should continue in the legislation concerning the industrial development bank.
I conclude by saying again that we approve the enlargement of lending opportunities of this bank. I compliment the administration for enlarging the area of entitlement of businesses which may obtain loans from the bank. Last year, and I think the year before, I had on the order paper a

bill to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act for the purpose of enlarging borrowers' entitlement. This measure goes even further than my amendment.
While we approve this bill in principle,
I do hope the Minister of Finance will explain to the house how the capital is to be provided; how the loan money is to be provided; whether or not this involves real money provided by the government in addition to the statement on non-budgetary transactions and net cash requirements referred to at page 6666 of Hansard; whether this involves printing press money, and so on.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

Mr. Speaker, if no one else wishes to take part in the debate there are a few observations I should like to make to support what has been said by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River, particularly with respect to the regional aspect of the activities of the industrial development bank.
I recall very well that when the industrial development bank was first established in 1944 by the Mackenzie King government as part of its program for reconstruction after the war and for maintenance of the full employment which continued after the war until 1957 there was a great deal of criticism from those hon. gentlemen opposite now sitting on the treasury benches but who were on this side of the house at that time. There were a few of them. Their criticism was that this was more or less socialistic; that it was interfering with the legitimate scope of the chartered banks and other lending institutions, and that it should be viewed with a great deal of concern.
Notwithstanding those criticisms the Mackenzie King government went ahead with this legislation. We find, as in so many other things, that after four years of floundering around in uncertainty this government comes along and says these excellent measures that were put into operation by the Liberal government can now be improved and extended. They hope that by doing that they will get for themselves the credit for these measures.
We get this from these great latter day apostles of free enterprise. Perhaps that slogan we got from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) after his return from London on that occasion when he had to have two planes to make sure he got here for the Tory convention-that slogan of free enterprise against socialism-did not apply in this field. I say this because we now find these great apostles of free enterprise, led by that great champion of Bay street, the present Minister of Finance, (Mr. Fleming), asking us to extend the scope of the industrial development bank
3, 1S61
Industrial Development Bank Act across the whole spectrum of lending for every conceivable legitimate purpose. I assume certain illegitimate activities would still be viewed with some disfavour in the lending policy of the industrial development bank.
I think it is worth underlining that there is quite a difference between the profession of hon. gentlemen opposite on the hustings in these great windy speeches that are made from time to time and the kind of measures they bring before us in this house.
We are listening to one now.

This measure was designed originally-and I trust it will be used in the future-only to supplement the existing private lending institutions. I do not think, with the bankrupt state of the treasury of this country at the present time, the government would be justified in seeking to supplant private lending institutions.
The minister made that all clear the other day.

The minister's words are so inconsistent with the conduct of the government that there are very few objective people in this country who pay much attention any more to the minister's words. We are seeking to find out what the line of action of the minister is going to be, not his words.
It seems to me the industrial development bank has filled and will continue to fill a useful purpose in providing lending money in a field that is at the present time not adequately covered by any of the existing private institutions. But I do not think that in a desperate effort to regain the confidence of certain sections of the community, which this government has so obviously lost, it should with this or any other institution indulge in reckless lending of public money for unsound projects. I think that kind of warning needs to be made at a time when we approve in principle what is after all only an extension of a Liberal measure. Mr. Speaker, there are certain other observations I have to make. In order to be consecutive in dealing with them, may I call it six o'clock? I see it is six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 7.30 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for dinner I had just concluded certain general observations of a more or
7442	HOUSE OF
Industrial Development Bank, Act less historical character about the industrial development bank and had recalled that it was part of a great program for the transformation of our economy from wartime to peacetime under Mr. Mackenzie King, Mr. Ilsley and Mr. C. D. Howe, which worked perhaps better than any similar transformation in any other country of the world, and which laid the foundation for 12 years of full employment in this country and a steadily expanding economy which, unfortunately, has not been continued in the past four years.
I also pointed out that at the time the industrial development bank was established those of the hon. gentlemen opposite who were here at that time had very grave misgivings about it because they regarded it as a rather dangerous experiment of state intervention in the field of lending. It is interesting to note now that they are seeking to expand its powers under the flag of free enterprise.
I did not rise primarily to give this historical review and to put this in its proper perspective so much as to refer to one difficulty inherent in the Canadian economy and in the nature of our country, and to draw attention to the fact that we have constantly to take thought to overcome this difficulty. That difficulty is that there is in our financial and commercial world a constant tendency to centralize, which a wise government presided over by wise ministers and by a wise treasury should always seek to offset. This has had to be done in the fields of taxation through equalization; and in the field of making capital available, it has to be done through a great variety of devices, of which the industrial development bank is one.
If the industrial development bank is to be governed by purely commercial criteria in the allotment of its loans it will in fact be doing little more than duplicating or replacing private lending institutions. If it is to perform a useful function in our society it will have to do more than supply middle term capital which was one of the original purposes. It will have to seek to provide capital in such areas and ways that it will tend to offset to some degree the tendency to financial centralization which is, as I say, a thoroughly natural feature of our economy, but one which, if we are to have a healthy economy with reasonable equality of opportunity and advantage across the country we must constantly seek to offset.
In suggesting that I am not suggesting any argument on behalf of state ownership or anything that may even be vaguely described as socialism. I merely suggest that the principle of equalization, which has been followed by every constructive government from


Sir John A. Macdonald down to the present, is one which should constantly and conscientiously be followed.
I know as well as anyone how difficult it is to do this effectively because there is no doubt that, other things being equal, it is much easier to start an effective industry within 40 miles of Montreal or Toronto than within 40 miles of St. John's, Newfoundland, or in the province of Saskatchewan, or some other relatively sparsely settled part of the country where one must overcome the disabilities of transportation, small markets, and so on.
As I say, if the industrial development bank is to be governed by purely commercial criteria, practically all its lending will be done in central Canada and that is certainly not desirable. I suggest it is very important that it should focus its interest primarily on two sectors of the economy. First, it should focus on small businesses which are not operating on a scale where they can go themselves directly into the capital market offering bonds or debentures, or where they have other forms of ready access to private capital. It should concentrate primarily on those businesses which are not large enough to bear the additional expense of floating their own loans, but which are soundly run and which have real opportunities for expansion and which can fill a need sometimes very much more effectively than much larger businesses because there are people involved who are more directly interested in getting results. In other words, properly conceived this can promote real private enterprise as opposed to large scale corporate endeavour in a very effective way. That is one area.
The other area is in respect to regional development. It is even harder to accomplish results in this area. Very often the scale of loans required by businesses in this field is so low that it really would not be worth while for the bank to engage in the activity. I know this from personal experience which I have had with potential borrowers in the province of Newfoundland. Two or three cases have come to my notice over the years I have represented Bonavista-Twillingate. I know that these applications were made to the industrial development bank and the view taken by the bank was that these looked like pretty sound propositions but the amount of the loan was so small and the cost of necessary supervision of the loan so high that it was not worth while to make the loan. Yet at the same time these loans were required for a longer period than that for which the chartered banks normally lend. I do feel that in this field some technique should be worked out which I do not think has been worked out yet. This

need is not being met-though another very important one is by these government guaranteed loans to small businesses that were inaugurated a few months ago-and it will not be met by the industrial development bank under its existing practices. But I would think there might be some possibility of having some co-operative arrangement between the chartered banks and the industrial development bank whereby the chartered banks, which have their branches all over the country could act as agents for the industrial development bank in assessing and supervising some of the smaller loans so that it would not be necessary for the industrial development bank to have a staff of its own for the purpose and all the travelling expenses and other charges of that sort which would increase the overhead and make unsatisfactory top heavy arrangements. If the commercial banker felt that the risk was good enough that his bank was prepared to provide the annual working capital for the business which was required and if he were satisfied that it looked like a business that was good for expansion, the industrial development bank would not just automatically take their word but would at least count on the chartered banks or credit unions in certain cases supervising these loans and in that way cut down the cost of the overhead.
There is one thing that I think anyone who has had any experience in government or with any large scale organization must become impressed with all the time and that is the great necessity of avoiding unnecessary overhead expenditures. There is always a tendency to have too many people producing too many files and checking up too often. I sometimes think that we could reduce taxes and reduce the cost of government a great deal more if we were willing to take a chance a little oftener on some things and had far less of the accounting and checking than we have at the present time on small matters. I know, of course, what a scandal can be made if someone purloins $20 from the treasury, but sometimes you know you really wonder whether you should spend $500 or $1,000 a year on the off-chance that someone will get $20 from the treasury once in a while. A great deal of that sort of thing does go on in government no matter who is in the government.
As I say, if this industrial development bank, extending its scope over a much wider range of business, is going to have a real impact it has to take perhaps a little more risk than it has been taking up to now. The fact is, of course, it has been very well and prudently run by very able people. It is quite evident that the government must have that
Industrial Development Bank Act view because notwithstanding what the government is seeking to do with the president of the industrial development bank at the present time they still want the president of it to go on running the bank. I am not advocating recklessness or imprudence at all; quite the contrary. But I am saying that perhaps a somewhat greater degree of calculated risk will have to be taken if indeed these amendments are to realize that greater degree of expansion which Mr. Coyne was anxious to have when he recommended these changes to the government, which the government has now seen fit to bring before us and ask us to approve.
As I say, the measure of the expansion will be the measure of a reasonable degree of risk taken in this venture. I suggest that where the greatest risks should be taken are in the two areas I have mentioned: first, in the provision of capital for relatively small businesses that have not got the scope, and necessarily have not got it, to raise capital that large businesses do have by floating their own bonds and debentures; second, in seeking to offset this tendency toward commercial and financial centralization which is, as I say, an inevitable aspect of the kind of country we have and which it should always be the duty of every statesmanlike government to seek to offset.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few observations on the bill which relates to a subject that has been of interest to myself and I know to a number of other hon. members of the house. It has been pointed out by the previous speaker and by others that the industrial development bank as it exists at the present time and as it has existed over the years has not been entirely satisfactory. While it may have been in the first place, in later years I do not feel that it has met the needs of the community or of the country and for that reason these very welcome changes to the act have been made.
It has always been my understanding that the original intention of the act was that the industrial development bank should supplement ordinary commercial credit channels. However, certainly in many instances, this has not been the case. I know that many of us around here have heard that it is much easier for companies to get loans from the commercial banks than it ever was to get them from the industrial development bank in the past. I heard one person put it rather picturesquely. He said it was easier to get teeth out of a hen than it was to get a loan from the industrial development bank. That may perhaps be stretching the point a little
7444	HOUSE OF
Industrial Development Bank Act but it does reflect the view of the public in general toward this institution.
Other hon. members have pointed out some of the advantages of the changes in the act. I do not wish to take up the time of the house in dwelling on and repeating them. It is very-fine and very commendable indeed to have all businesses included. The amendments to the act will be of great assistance. They will provide much greater assistance to small and medium-sized businesses and the like. There is one important point that I do not think has been dealt with. I refer to the fact that under the new terms, as I undersand them, we will be able not only to provide additional financing for the development of our resources but will also help to keep our resources in Canadian hands, which is certainly most important.
There are a great many resources in this country. Our primary industries include mining in all its branches, forest industries and the like. Many of these industries have very good propositions from time to time but many have difficulty in raising capital through the ordinary commercial channels. As all hon. members know, there can be only a limited amount of risk capital available in a country like Canada because of our small population and the limited savings of our people. Countries such as the United States and others in Europe have much larger amounts of money available for risk capital. Many parts of the world, for political reasons and others, are not places in which people wish to invest their money. I think everybody knows this is a self-evident fact, but I think it sometimes does not hurt to repeat it. There are few countries in the world where people from abroad can invest their money with a great degree of safety. Canada is certainly one of those countries, probably the leading one. In many other parts of the world where people used to invest risk capital they are not anxious to do so now. Some governments have recently become pretty nationalistic and are expropriating capital, and the political climate in those countries is not good for such ventures. As a result people from abroad are looking to this country, and have been as we all know, as a place in which to invest risk capital. I should like to cite one example. I will not name the company because that would probably not be fair. In 1958 a company was formed in one of the eastern Canadian provinces and it had very large proven deposits of a highly valuable mineral. It was a little difficult to obtain credit from the normal sources at that time for reasons which hon. members will know, and this particular company applied to the industrial development bank for assistance.


It is my understanding that, to say the least, they were given a very cursory hearing and turned down.
The result was that this particular mining company had to turn to United States and European capital which was obtained very quickly, but the situation now is that ownership and control of this great and very valuable resource is completely in foreign hands. What is more, the terms under which capital was borrowed to develop the mine were such that in the opinion of many the resource was virtually stolen.
It is just this kind of thing that the amendments to the act will now prevent. They will do so in two ways. In one case it may be done by the guaranteeing of the bonds of a company, as is already done by some provincial governments, and if the industrial development bank can guarantee the bonds of a company it may provide sufficient capital to go ahead with the enterprise. In the case of a larger enterprise, as may well happen on many occasions, the fact that the bonds and perhaps other current and long term liabilities of the company are guaranteed will greatly facilitate the sale of common or preferred shares in such a company because once the long or short term liabilities are guaranteed by the industrial development bank the element of risk disappears to a great extent with the result that additional capital is made more easily available.
There is always a limited amount of risk capital available in a country like Canada but there is always additional capital available for less risky projects. If the liabilities of these companies which are attempting to develop our resources should be guaranteed, it would make it much easier for them to obtain additional capital right here in Canada rather than having to go abroad to find capital, thus losing control of the resource as took place in the example to which I referred. As I have already said, I think the amendments to the act are most commendable and will do a great deal to develop our own resources and keep them in the hands of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) makes a speech I wonder whether I could put a question to him which he could answer in the course of his remarks. In view of the character of the bill and the fact that it is of considerable importance and has many clauses, it would seem to me that the proper course in accordance with regular practice would be for the bill to be sent to the banking and commerce committee. In that event I would hope it would be possible for

us to ask the president of the industrial development bank to come before that committee to give his views with regard to the bill and possibly, if the minister would graciously allow, his comments on other matters as well. At any rate, it might be possible for certain members of that committee, who are alert, vigilant and concerned with the public interest, to put questions to him on matters that might have some relationship to the industrial development bank bill.

I take it this is the measure that provides for an increase in the resources of the bank from $160 million to $400 million as announced in the budget. The minister will remember that at one time he announced a policy having to do with assistance over a period of one year to industries which would locate in depressed areas. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must confess to some surprise at some of the statements that have been made in the course of this debate having regard to the course of the debate at the resolution stage on June 30. I began by being surprised at the views expressed by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith). He may not have been aware that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) speaking on the resolution stage of this measure on June 30, said, as found at page 7312 of Hansard:
.. . we on this side have been advocating for some time now an expansion of the functions and activities of this very useful piece of machinery ...
The hon. member for Ottawa West expressed some concern at the removal of the limitations written into the present act and defining those industries that may qualify for loans from the industrial development bank. He seemed to expect that the bank was now going to lend money to race courses.
The act has hitherto defined in fairly explicit terms those industrial enterprises which qualify for loans under the act. There are four categories of them and in the course of administration those categories have become rather rigidly interpreted. There have been many requests for the removal of those rigidities and a widening of the scope of those industries which qualify for loans from the bank. This is part of the background.
When the government proposes in this measure to remove the existing limitations on the industries which qualify, it is not necessary for the hon. member to assume that the result is going to be the throwing around of public money on things like race courses. There are many enterprises that certainly regard themselves as equally worthy of loans from the industrial development bank as those that have been defined hitherto as qualifying. There have been many of them. For instance, rural telephone companies have not qualified. Then, there are the enterprises that are engaged in the tourist industry. There have been many requests for loans for motels, hotels and tourist establishments, and so one could go on. I mention these examples, Mr. Speaker, to disabuse the minds of hon. members of the idea that the enlargement of the scope of qualifying industrial enterprises under this bill is intended to embrace things that might be regarded by some people as frivolous. This is a serious attempt to make the industrial development bank more serviceable to the Canadian economy.
Now, sir, it should not be thought, either, that the bank in exercising the wide powers conferred upon it under this measure is going to throw to the winds those proper considerations and that discretion which any banker ought to observe. I have been at pains to

Industrial Development Bank Act stress this fact both in the budget speech and in speaking to the resolution on June 30. The bank must still use a banker's judgment and decide whether or not applicants are really creditworthy. In this regard, let me say that there is here no thought of just casting away the proper restraint.
However, at the same time I must say, hearkening to some of the comments made by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) that there has been not a little criticism directed at the operations of the industrial development bank. It is the hope of the government that with the enlargement of the powers under this act, the enlargement of the lending resources of the bank and the enlargement of the definition of industrial enterprises which may qualify for loans under the act, the bank will be in a position, as I have said, to be more serviceable to the Canadian economy.
There is no thought, Mr. Speaker, of having the bank duplicate existing credit facilities. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) evidently was not acquainted with what I endeavoured to say on this matter at the resolution stage on June 30. I was at some pains then to stress the fact that this institution, because it has access to public funds, should not be duplicating the facilities offered by private institutions. I recall to the minds of hon. members the fact that these safeguards are written right into this act itself. This is not something that is left to the good judgment of those who are administering the affairs of the bank. This is a safeguard that is written right into the terms of the act itself and it abides there. It is not changed by this present amending bill. Section 15 of the act reads:
(1) Subject to section 14, where In the opinion of the board
(a)	a person is engaged or about to engage in an industrial enterprise in Canada,
(b)	credit or other financial resources would not otherwise be available on reasonable terms and conditions,
An applicant who goes to the industrial development bank must establish, and it is proper that he should establish, that credit or other financial resources are not otherwise available to him on reasonable terms and conditions. If he is able to obtain commercial credit from a chartered bank, that is where he should go. If a large industry is able to meet its capital needs in the financial market, it is to the financial market that it should go. This institution is intended, and in its functions and scope is still intended, to fill what is otherwise a gap in the credit institutions of this country. It is not intended to duplicate the functions of the chartered banks in extending commercial credit for short

periods. It is not intended to duplicate or provide substitute credit facilities for those larger institutions which are in a position to raise money by bond or debenture issues on the market. This institution is intended principally to provide for those small and medium size institutions, loans in an area and for a term not otherwise available.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) asked about the application of the lending provisions of this act in regions where there has been an inadequate development of secondary industry. He has not acquainted himself with what I endeavoured to say on this subject at the resolution stage on June 30. At that time we heard a very effective plea by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacLellan) for the exercise of the functions of the bank in relation to assistance for the development of secondary industries in areas like his in Nova Scotia. In commenting on the submission made by the hon. member, I was at pains to stress that this ought to be regarded as one of the functions of the industrial development bank. I alluded to the fact that in the last five years the number of local offices of the industrial development bank has been enlarged from four to thirteen. This enlargement has been carried out with a view to making the services of the bank available in those regions on a much more local basis than had previously been possible.
For my part, I welcome this expansion of the localizing effect of the increase in the number of branches. It will enable those who are giving local administration to the affairs of the bank to be more intelligently acquainted with the needs of the local areas. I entirely endorse the plea made on Friday by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond, that the functions of this bank should be directed consciously toward assisting in the provision of the needed credit for the development of secondary industry in those areas.
There were several other questions asked about the way in which the increase in capital is to be met. The answer is right in the terms of the bill itself, but the rules of the house preclude me from drawing attention to the specific provisions of the clauses of the bill. However, the answers are there. The purpose of this measure was praised by all sections of the house last Friday. I hope the measure will continue to enjoy the support of hon. members in all parts of the house.

I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to deal with something that took place during my absence when the minister was making his concluding remarks on second reading. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Stick to the facts.

I will stick to the facts and I will debate the point. It is relevant to this clause. I will insist on the right to have the point stated. Although I have not had an opportunity of seeing the minister's remarks


in print because it is not possible to do so under the rules of the house, I am told that the minister represented me as having taken a position that was inconsistent with that which was taken by the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke on second reading of this bill. However unpleasant it may be to the minister to hear this, the rest of the committee is entitled to hear it. May I say that the position I took was wholly consistent with that of the Leader of the Opposition. If the minister had done me the honour of paying attention to my remarks when I was making them, he would have known this. I had made it clear that I thought the objective of the bill was wholly desirable but I expressed regret that, in achieving that desirable objective or seeking to bring it about, he had expressed the bill in the language used in it.
I had gone on to point out that the widening of the activities of the industrial development bank took place under this bill in two main ways. One was by increasing the amount of money available for them and the other was in increasing the types of business or enterprise to which they could make loans by redefinition of the term "industrial enterprise" in clause 1 of the bill. I had expressed regret that in that redefinition he had chosen this particular method because, in addition to achieving the wholly desirable objective of making more money available to this bank for the laudable purposes for which it is provided, he had done it by way of making any industry, trade or other business available as potential borrowers.
I had pointed out that this use of the word any had opened up the possibility of using taxpayers' money by way of loan for certain types of business which did not contribute anything substantial to the economy of this country or to the development of the country and which I was sure hon. members on all sides of the house would not wish to see helped with taxpayers' money. That was the point I had made. There is nothing in that point inconsistent with the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition on second reading. I thought I owed it to the committee to make that perfectly clear.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, I regret that I was not able to be in the house when the minister was making his remarks so that I could have heard them precisely, but with the vicissitudes of the business of the house being conducted as it is and, as perhaps of necessity it must be, during the closing days of this part of the session, I could not help being absent. I hope the apology in that respect is accepted.

Mr. Chairman, I was absent for 40 minutes attending the same committee

as the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. I have just one question to ask the minister. Was this amending bill, and particularly the clause that applies to all businesses without limitation, introduced by the government on the recommendation of the president of the industrial development bank or is it the result of the minister's own observation of circumstances in the country and the application of the industrial development bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is introduced as a result of a government decision but there have been discussions with the authorities of the bank.

Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago I raised a matter to which the minister did not immediately address himself. He gave the impression that he did not regard the suggestion as a serious one and dismissed it somewhat summarily. I believe it is an important suggestion and I am going to renew it at this time.
First of all I want to say that, as the Leader of the Opposition indicated, the principle of this bill is one which we strongly support, not only because of the improvements that are made in the operations of the industrial development bank but because our own experience has indicated that the bill in its original form served a useful purpose and in the light of existing economic conditions in the country the improvements are calculated to meet the new economic situation that faces us.
There have been many complaints, of course, about the administration of the industrial development bank. It has been charged by would-be borrowers and others that the bank exercised a restrictionist policy and on that account it was not possible for them to get the kind of credit they required to enable them to maintain their industrial enterprises.
It would be interesting, in the light of the kind of experience that the bank will have in the future, for hon. members to know in much greater detail than we have had from the minister what has been the experience of the bank in the past with regard to this matter. There is an office of the industrial development bank in the city of London which I suppose is intended to serve the district from London to Windsor and from London to Hamilton. The minister, in mentioning that there would be four new branches in the bank's operations, did not say what other places-

speechtext: I said that in the last five years the number of branches had increased from four to 13.

I thank the minister. He says now that the number of branches which have been in existence will continue and there will be no addition to their number. I had hoped that in view of the fact that an effort is being made in my own city of Windsor to get new industry, and particularly a whole series of small industries, the importance of that city would be recognized in any new branches that were going to be set up. However the minister indicates that there are not going to be any new branches.
As I say, there have been complaints about the criteria established by the bank in the past in the loans it has made to enterprises covered by this bill. The minister has said that a new spirit is to be engendered in the administration of the industrial development bank; an attempt is going to be made to recognize special conditions and special situations. One would hope that the special situations the hon. gentleman had in mind would be those chronically depressed areas in the country that come within the mischief of the minister's anaemic double depreciation program announced in the baby budget and about which we have heard so little ever since.
Because we want to make sure that the criteria to be established in the future meet the conditions and the objectives laid down by the minister in the statement he made a few moments ago I think we must have more information than is now available to us. It is all very well for a minister of the crown piloting a bill of this sort through the house to speak generously and perhaps even extravagantly of his intentions. It is all very well for the Minister of Finance to say that under this administration an attempt is going to be made to bring the potential power of this measure into areas where such credit has not been available at the hands of the crown. However, one often finds that the declarations made by members of a government before

Industrial Development Bank Act an act is passed are not in practice fully supported by those who are called upon to administer the act once it is passed. That certainly might well be the case in the future. One way of determining that would be to know in advance what criteria are going to be employed. Is special attention going to be paid to chronically unemployed areas? Is an attempt going to be made to use this measure to provide for an alleviation of unemployment in areas that are depressed? 'Is this bill really going to meet the very laudable objectives which the minister has postulated? I suggest that one way of getting an answer to this series of questions would be for the minister to agree to send this bill to the banking and commerce committee.
The minister has turned down that request. He made the perfectly obvious remark that the bill would ultimately go to the committee of the whole. Of course every hon. member was aware of that procedure. The question was whether the bill would go to a standing committee of the house, and that is certainly not an unusual request. Bills much less complicated than this which have been introduced by the minister have been sent to the banking and commerce committee. The minister the other day sent to that committee a group of bills having to do with trust companies and the like. We had a very valuable discussion in that committee. That discussion certainly elicited information which had not been forthcoming from the minister in his statements in this house.
I am sure that if we had before that committee on this bill the new directors, particularly the new directors who are now in the government service, as well as the old directors now in the government service, we would have a much more detailed description of their intended functions. We would have a more precise appreciation of the criteria which they would employ than we have obtained from the minister. We would have an opportunity of ascertaining in greater detail and with greater precision why loans in the past, under some of the very same authority now provided in this bill, have not been extended. We would be able particularly to ascertain what are going to be the future intentions of the directors in this regard.
The deputy minister of trade and commerce, or whoever happens to be the deputy minister at the time, is going to be made a director. I think that is a wise suggestion. It would be very useful to have him give us an indication of the plans, in the light of the pronouncement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to the increase in Canada's export trade, because many of the industries that can benefit from this kind of legislation will be industries, as


I know from my own community, of the smaller type seeking outlets in Canada's external markets.
It would also, of course, be interesting to learn from the president of the bank what his experience has been with regard to the administration of this act and the criteria he, as president of the bank, envisages for the operations in the future. After all, the governor of the Bank of Canada continues to be the president of the industrial development bank. Notwithstanding the vicissitudes which may have crept into the structure of the government of Canada within recent weeks the present governor of the Bank of Canada continues to be the president of the industrial development bank.
We are entitled as members of parliament to have from that individual an accounting of his stewardship and administration as head of this bank as well as an indication of the kind of policy he and his colleagues on the board of directors intend to pursue in furthering the objectives of this bank in respect of which the lending facilities are to be increased from $100 million to $400 million. That represents a very large increase and surely we are entitled to have from those who are going to administer this an indication of how they are going to apply it particularly in the chronically unemployed areas such as those I have mentioned.
It cannot be argued that the minister has satisfied the committee or the house in respect to the kind of question I am asking now. Surely he cannot deny us the opportunity of eliciting further information in this regard. What objection can there be to having this bill sent to the banking and commerce committee in accordance with our traditional practice? I can very well envisage what the minister would say if he were in the opposition and this situation were confronting another administration. I can recall some of the declamations which he has made in the past in respect to matters involving the same kind of principle that now agitates me. How he would have complained about the treatment of parliament by the government if the government of that day had restricted its responses only to those who were actually in the executive arm of government.
The Minister of Finance is a busy man and could not possibly know all that one would expect an administrator of the industrial development bank to know. This measure can be a very important measure for improving our economic conditions, for alleviating unemployment, for setting in motion the productive processes of much new industry in Canada, but the only way that can be done

is by industry learning, through the members of the banking and commerce committee, what the intentions of the administrators are.
It is all very well for the minister to take the position that he has laid down the very broad lines involved in this legislation but it is not the broad lines we want; we want the details which the Minister of Finance has not given. He has spoken in laudatory terms of the general intentions but he has not given us any indication as to the character of industry that will be assisted. He has not told us of the percentage of an applicant's capital set-up which will be required, for instance, to make it possible for that industry to qualify. What are the criteria in that regard? How much equity will an industry be required to have before that industry will be able to qualify for a loan under this act?

The directors, other than the governor and deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance and the deputy minister of trade and commerce, are entitled to receive for attendance at meetings of the board and meetings of the executive committee such fees as may be fixed by the by-laws of the bank, but the aggregate amount of the fees paid to all directors exclusive of expenses shall not exceed twenty thousand dollars in any fiscal year.
In the clause we are now discussing, clause 6, provision is made that the Bank of Canada shall subscribe for the said 500,000 shares at par and shall pay the amount of such subscription at such times and in such amounts as the board may determine. The present governor of the bank is a member of that board. The present governor of the bank is covered by the provisions of clause 3 which I have already recited. The minister owes it to the committee to say whether or not he has confidence in this governor or he has no right to bring forward this bill which provides for the inclusion of the present governor. The minister cannot for one moment argue that he has the right to anticipate events which may or may not take place. The minister must assume that the law of the land shall be respected and the law of the land makes provision for the governor of the Bank of Canada as president of the industrial development bank.
A few moments ago the minister made the argument that I was engaged in an argument of fiction. I say to him that there is no fiction in clause 3. There is no fiction in clause 6. The provisions therein contained deal with the Bank of Canada and with the governor of the bank. The minister must tell the committee now whether or not he has sufficient

My ministers are convinced that additional medium term credit facilities for small businesses would enable many private projects to go forward this winter all across Canada, providing substantial additional employment.
